paragraphs.heading: What a rift valley is
paragraphs.text: A rift valley is a lowland with a linear shape that lies between several highlands or mountain ranges. It is produced by the action of a geologic rift. Rifts form when the lithosphere is pulled apart by extensional tectonics.

paragraphs.heading: What happens to the valley
paragraphs.text: Once the long depression exists, the forces of erosion may deepen it further. More generally, the valley is likely to fill with sedimentary deposits that come from the flanks of the rift and the surrounding areas. In many cases rift lakes form. The East African Rift is among the best known examples of this process. A rift valley often comes with a number of adjoining subsidiary valleys, and these are typically counted as part of the main rift valley geologically.

paragraphs.heading: On the sea floor
paragraphs.text: On Earth, rifts can occur at any elevation, from the sea floor up to plateaus and mountain ranges, and in either continental or oceanic crust. The most extensive rift valley follows the crest of the mid-ocean ridge system. It is a result of sea floor spreading. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East Pacific Rise are examples of this type of rift.

paragraphs.heading: On the continents
paragraphs.text: A failed arm of a triple junction, called an aulacogen, is what produced many of the continental rift valleys that exist. Three continental rifts are currently active: the East African Rift, the Rio Grande rift and the Baikal Rift Zone. A fourth, the West Antarctic Rift System, may be active as well. In these, entire tectonic plates, not just the crust, are breaking apart and forming new plates. Continental rifts that keep going will eventually turn into oceanic rifts.

paragraphs.heading: Rifts made by sideways faults
paragraphs.text: Other rift valleys come from bends or discontinuities in strike-slip faults, which are faults that move horizontally. When a bend or discontinuity points the same way as the relative motion along the fault, extension occurs. On a right lateral-moving fault, for example, a bend to the right stretches the area of the irregularity, and it subsides as a result. Many geologists today hold that the Dead Sea lies in a rift of this kind, produced where the Dead Sea Transform fault, which moves left-laterally, has a leftward discontinuity. Fault-caused extension like this commonly happens on a small scale, producing features such as sag ponds or landslides.

paragraphs.heading: Home of great lakes
paragraphs.text: Many of the world's largest lakes sit in rift valleys. Lake Baikal in Siberia lies in an active rift valley. It is the deepest lake in the world, and it has the greatest volume, holding 20% of all the liquid freshwater on Earth. Lake Tanganyika is second on both measures and sits in the Albertine Rift, the westernmost arm of the East African Rift. The largest freshwater lake by area, Lake Superior in North America, sits in the Midcontinent Rift, which is ancient and dormant.

paragraphs.heading: Rift valleys on other worlds
paragraphs.text: Rift valleys are also known on other terrestrial planets and on natural satellites. Planetary geologists believe that Valles Marineris on Mars, which is 4,000 km long, is a large rift system. Some satellites have prominent rift valleys too, such as Ithaca Chasma on Tethys, in the Saturn system, which is 2,000 km long. A recent study suggests the Moon has a complex system of ancient rift valleys, among them Vallis Rheita and Vallis Alpes. In the Uranus system, large chasma are thought to be giant rift valley systems, and a notable one is Messina Chasma on Titania, 1492 km long.
